text:
Ravi was late for the bus, with a napkin still stuck in his hand from breakfast. His thumb was sore from typing all morning, so he talked to his phone instead.

'Mute notifications,' he said.

The phone understood that he wanted the alerts from his social media app to go quiet. It turned them off and said they would stay off until he asked for them again. Ravi nodded and jogged toward the stop.

Then he remembered his cousin's photo from last night. 'Like it,' he said. The phone found the newest post from his cousin and tapped the like button. A small heart showed up under the picture.

'Now stop the video,' he added, because a clip was still playing on the screen. The phone paused it. Ravi smiled, put the napkin in his pocket, and got on the bus just in time.

Mrs. Alvarez sat at her desk with a pencil and a crossword. It was past seven, and her stomach had been growling for an hour.

'My fridge is empty and my feet are tired,' she said to her tablet.

She never said the word dinner, but the assistant understood. It opened her food delivery app and showed her the last thing she had ordered, a bowl of noodle soup from a place on Maple Street. 'Same again?' it asked.

'Yes, please. That was easy last time,' she said.

The assistant placed the order. It explained that the restaurant did not ship far, so a rider from nearby would bring the soup in about twenty minutes. Mrs. Alvarez went back to her crossword. When the bell rang, the soup was still hot.

Jo was texting her friend Priya when she remembered the tomato plants. They had looked dry all week. She picked up her phone and typed, 'the tomatoes look sad. they need more water.'

The assistant understood that Jo wanted the back garden sprinklers to run for longer. It did not ask any more questions. It changed the sprinkler plan from ten minutes to twenty-five minutes and told her the new time would start tomorrow morning.

Jo wrote back, 'ok thx.' Then she remembered the garden party on Saturday and asked what the weather would be like. The assistant said the day would be dry and sunny, so she could dress lightly. Jo sent Priya a thumbs up and went back to their chat.

A bike route is a path from one place to another that suits people on bicycles. It is for staying on quiet streets and cycle paths instead of busy roads. People often change a route to fit their day. They might say make it shorter, avoid the steep hills, or find me something flat. A club might invite friends for a Sunday ride and share a recent route that ends at a cafe with warm pancakes. Riders also ask about their ride afterwards. How far did I go? How fast was I on the last hill? How long did it take? A good route is easy to follow and fits the time you have.

They want the assistant to wake them with an alarm.
wake me at seven
alarm for tomorrow at seven please
I have an early train, so can you get me up tomorrow at seven
set my automatic wake-up for tomorrow at seven
ring me out of bed at seven, and make it a slow, gentle sound like waves on sand

make sure I do not sleep in tomorrow, I have to be out of the house by eight
buzz me at 7 tomorrow

Dana was packing lunches while the kids ran around looking for their shoes. The bus was due in five minutes. As always, she felt a small worry about the house.

'I never know if the garage is shut when we fly out of here in the morning,' she said to the speaker on the shelf.

The assistant took this as a question about the garage door. It checked the door sensor and said the door was still open. 'Do you want me to close it?' it asked.

'Yes, please,' said Dana.

The door came down. The assistant told her it was closed and that the front door was locked too. It was so easy that Dana laughed. She grabbed the lunches, counted three kids, and hurried out into the cold.

Most people use a phone or a screen to find a film. You can look for what is on tonight, watch a trailer, or check the cinema times near your home. People change a few things when they ask. They might say show me something funny, find a film that is not scary, or what is on after dinner. Some people hate loud action films, and others only want a spicy thriller. Families often ask for something short, so the little ones can stay awake. A cinema may also tell you how long a film is. A long one can run almost three hours, which feels like carrying a kilogram of popcorn on your lap.

Grandpa Leo sat in the basement next to the old dehumidifier. It had an automatic switch that turned it on and off, and he did not care for the noise it made. Upstairs, his grandsons were coming for supper.

'Get us two large pizzas, plain cheese, from the place on Elm Street,' he told his phone.

The assistant opened the food delivery app and found the shop. It put two large cheese pizzas in the basket and asked, 'Would you like to leave a tip for the driver?'

'Twenty percent, please. They drive in all kinds of weather,' said Leo.

The assistant added the tip and told him the pizzas would arrive in about thirty minutes. Leo turned off the basement light and went up to set the table.

Grandma Rosa was excited. Her granddaughter had a school concert tonight, and she wanted to study the parking situation before she left the house.

'Find me a parking spot near the school hall for seven o'clock,' she told her phone.

The assistant searched and showed two car parks close to the hall. One was free and one cost three dollars an hour.

Then Rosa remembered how crowded it always got. 'No, wait. Make that six thirty. I want to be early and find a good seat.'

The assistant understood she meant the arrival time, not the concert time. It changed the plan to six thirty, picked the free car park, and said it would remind her to leave at six. Rosa picked up her coat and her camera and smiled.

Maya got home after a long night shift. Her eyes were heavy, and she wanted to lie down, but she knew she would forget something important.

'Remind me to take my pants to the cleaner when I walk past the square this afternoon,' she said to her phone. 'Don't remind me tonight, and please don't make it loud. I'll be asleep.'

The assistant understood that the reminder should happen at a place, not at a time. It set a reminder for when she was near the town square later that day. It also said it would not send anything tonight, and it turned off the sound for this reminder so it would only show a small message.

Maya thanked it, pulled the curtains shut, and fell asleep within a minute.

Food delivery lets you order a meal from a restaurant and have it brought to your door. You pick the dishes, check the address, and see how long it will take. People change things a lot. They ask for less spice, an extra side, or a later time. Many people owe a small thank you to the driver, so they add a tip. My uncle is careful with his orders. He says he wants it hot, not too salty, and at the door by seven. If the food is late, you can ask where the driver is. If you made a mistake, you can say cancel that order or change the address.

We measure things so that other people know how big, heavy or hot something is. Sometimes people use different units, like meters and feet, or kilograms and pounds. Say you are on a video call and tell your sister that the bathroom is two meters wide. She only knows feet, so she asks, how much is that? You unmute and say it is about six and a half feet. People ask for these changes with words like how many feet is that, what is it in pounds, or give me that in Celsius. Even a shallow pool has to be measured. The shallow end might be four feet deep, which is a little more than a meter.

A kitchen has many machines that help us cook. An oven heats food, a kettle boils water, and a coffee machine makes a hot drink. A dishwasher cleans plates while you rest. On a sunny morning, many people turn on the kettle first. They change the temperature, the time, or the program. They say things like bake it for ten more minutes, make the water hotter, or run the short wash. My dog likes to sit by the oven when something smells good. A heavy cast iron pan works on the stove and in the oven, so you can start it on the fire and finish it in the heat. Always wait for hot things to cool.

A podcast is a show you can listen to whenever you like. An audiobook is a book read aloud, often in chapters. Both remember where you stopped, so you do not have to wait or search when you come back. People use them on walks, on trains, and while they cook. They change a few things. They speed up a slow voice, jump to the next chapter, or go back thirty seconds to hear a sentence again. They say play faster, skip ahead, or where did I leave off? Your goal is to enjoy the story without trouble. If the end of a chapter is close, you can ask for one more episode before bed.

Tomas was a gardener, and on his lunch break he was writing a short note for the garden club. He sat on a bench with one tired foot on a bucket and spoke to his phone.

'How many words do I have so far?' he asked.

The assistant counted and said there were ninety-eight words. Tomas wanted the note to be short, so he said, 'Tell me if it goes over one hundred and twenty.' The assistant said it would.

He read the note on the screen. The letters were small, so he said, 'Raise the text size.' The assistant made the letters bigger. Tomas fixed one spelling mistake in the word tomatoes, and wrote about how healthy the roses looked this spring. Then he finished his sandwich.

Grandpa Ned could not sleep. The alarm clock beside his bed was so loud that he kept waking up half asleep, just waiting for it. He wanted a change, but he did not know how to explain it.

'The alarm is too loud,' he said to the speaker on the table. 'Make it half as loud, and start it softer.'

The assistant understood that he meant the morning alarm. It cut the volume to half and set the sound to rise slowly instead of starting at full strength. It also asked if he wanted the old alarm to stay, and Ned said no.

Before bed, the old clock was hidden in a drawer. Ned rolled over, closed his eyes, and slept all the way until the soft chime came.

Person: Please book me a taxi for tomorrow morning.
Assistant: Happy to. Where should the driver pick you up?
Person: At my house, of course.
Assistant: I do not know your address yet. Would you like me to save it for next time? What is it?
Person: Twelve Birch Lane. I want to get to the clinic twenty minutes before my visit.
Assistant: Thank you. What time is your visit?
Person: Ten o'clock.
Assistant: Then I will book a taxi for nine fifteen. The minimum fare is eight dollars. Shall I add a note for the driver?
Person: Yes, please say I walk slowly.

Priya came home after her night shift with her eyes half closed. In two days, her family would celebrate the winter holiday, and the house still had no lights. She dropped her bag on the sofa and spoke to the speaker.

'Play carols,' she said.

The assistant started a playlist of holiday songs at a low volume. Priya smiled. 'Lights on,' she said next. The assistant switched on the string of lights around the window. 'Timer ten,' she added. It set a timer for ten minutes, and Priya put a pan of potatoes on to fry, with the minimum of fuss. Her family and her whole network of cousins would be coming, and she wanted the first batch to be ready. When the timer rang, she was almost asleep, with the lights glowing behind her.

Every home uses electricity, and the amount changes with the day. Lights, the fridge, the heating and a laptop for homework all use some. Solar panels catch the sun, even on a pale winter day, and turn it into power for the house. People change their habits to save energy. They turn off lights, lower the heating, or run the washing machine at night when power is cheaper. They say things like how much power did I use today, switch off the lights downstairs, or cancel the heating for tonight. A small change each day can lower the bill. It also helps to know which machines use the most.

name: bedtime_story_picker
does: Picks a short bedtime story for a child, based on age and mood, and reads it aloud.
inputs: the child's age, and what kind of story they want
people say:
- tell the kids a story about a mountain
- something calm so she can fall asleep
- my son is five and wants a story about a train ride
- read us a cozy story, we are tired and comfortable in bed
- do you have a short tale with a friendly dragon

A radio brings voices and music from far away. You tune it to a station, and a calm voice reads the news, plays a song, or tells you the weather. Years ago, a waiter in a small cafe might turn the radio on for his customers. Today, many people ask a speaker to do it. They say put on the radio, find a news station, or turn it down a little. Some people whisper at night, so the sound must be low. Others want a different station for each part of the day. They say change the station, play something else, or what is this song? The radio is a simple way to hear what is happening.

Hana's laptop battery was at ten percent, and her meeting started in two minutes. Her baby was crying in the next room. She was a busy parent, and she had no time to waste.

'Join my work call,' she told her phone. The assistant opened the calendar, found the meeting and joined it. The video was bright, but the screen was a plain white page.

'Share my notes, but only half of the screen,' Hana said. 'And turn the volume down by half, the baby is loud.'

The assistant understood both parts. It set the call to share one half of her screen and lowered the volume. Then it reminded her to plug in the laptop. Hana set the charger on the floor beside her chair and joined the talk with a smile.

Hector was a cook, and his hands were tired from slicing onions all day. Tonight, he wanted to start a workout at home.

'Start a leg workout with three sets of ten squats,' he told his phone. A moment later he said, 'No, make it twelve, not ten.'

The assistant understood that he was fixing a number. It changed the plan to three sets of twelve and began a timer for the first set. It also asked about the rest, and Hector said sixty seconds.

Halfway through, his knee felt strange. 'That seems dangerous,' he said to the assistant. 'Should I stop?' The assistant said that a person should stop if something hurts, and it paused the workout. Hector sat down, drank some water, and tried again tomorrow.

Walter was not good with technology. He had a small speaker at home that his daughter had given him, and he rarely used it. Tonight he felt nervous. A holiday was starting tomorrow, and he had to travel early by train. The house was chilly, and the bed was cold.

He took a breath and said, 'set an alrm for six tomorrow.'

The speaker understood him well enough. It said, 'Alarm set for six in the morning.' Walter was surprised that it had worked. He asked, 'Can it make a loud noise?' The assistant said the alarm would ring until he said stop.

Walter smiled, put his bag by the door, and went to sleep under two blankets.

Cars need small things to keep them working. They need fuel, air in the tyres, and a little care. A car alarm makes a loud noise if someone tries to open the doors. You can also set a reminder alarm for when your parking time runs out. People change many things about their cars. They ask to warm up the engine before a cold trip, check the tyre pressure, or find out where they left the car. They say things like where did I park, how much fuel is left, or start the car. Friends sometimes split the cost of fuel on a long trip. A local garage can help when something looks wrong.

Ines was a shop owner, and she was excited because tonight was her first night away on holiday. She was locking the shop at the end of the day, and the street was quiet. She had a cookie in one hand and her phone in the other.

She typed in a hurry, 'turn on the alarm at the shpo.'

The assistant knew she meant the shop. It switched on the alarm and the door sensors. It also woke the camera at the back door. It told her, 'The shop alarm is on. Your cousin will arrive tomorrow at eight to open it.' Ines had asked it to tell him the code, and it had sent him a private message.

She finished her cookie, checked the lock once more, and went home to pack.

Sam was a busy parent who only had twenty minutes for exercise. The baby was asleep, and the kitchen floor was clean enough to stand on.

'Give me a short workout, medium speed, with double the squats from yesterday,' Sam said to the speaker.

The assistant remembered that Sam had done ten squats the day before. It made a plan with twenty squats, then push-ups and a short plank, and it set the pace to medium. It counted each round out loud.

Halfway through, Sam started to sing along to the song in the background and almost lost count. 'Do half again,' Sam gasped, meaning the last set. The assistant repeated half the set, which was ten. Sam wiped a mouth full of sweat on a towel and finished.

Omar was a driver who spent most of his week in the car. This morning he was waiting for a customer, and he wanted a few things done before the next trip. He did not want to turn the heater up himself.

'Warm up the front seats, and do not send me on the highway,' he said to the car's assistant. 'The fees are too high this week.'

The assistant understood both parts. It turned on the seat heaters. It also changed the route for the next ride so it used city streets, and it told him the ride would take eleven minutes longer. 'Is that okay?' it asked.

'Fine,' said Omar. The customer got in, and the car was warm and ready.

Accessibility settings help people use a phone or computer in the way that suits them. A person with weak eyes may want bigger text. Someone who cannot see the screen may want the device to read it aloud. Others may prefer to talk instead of tap. People change the settings with simple words. They say make the letters bigger, read this page to me, or dim the screen, it hurts my eyes. If a word is wrong, they can say no, that is not right, and say it again. Voice control lets a person open an app, call a friend, or turn a page without touching the device. These tools make the same device easier for everyone.

Some people wake up with a podcast every morning, and they know the voice better than their neighbors. A podcast app keeps a list of shows and plays the newest episode. In the summer, many people listen while they walk or sit in the garden. They often change how fast the voice talks. They say play it faster, slow it down, or go back thirty seconds. If a show is long, they may listen to half now and half later. The app remembers where you stopped. You can also say play the next episode, what is this one about, or stop this at the end of the chapter. A sleep timer will turn it off when you fall asleep.

Person: Fix the spelling in my letter and make the tone softer.
Assistant: Of course. Which letter do you mean? I see two drafts.
Person: The one to my landlord. I'm in a hurry.
Assistant: Got it. How soft would you like it? Polite, or very gentle?
Person: Polite is fine. Also tell me the word count. The paper fell on the floor and I can't read the old copy.
Assistant: The letter has one hundred and eighty words. I fixed three spelling mistakes and changed two hard sentences. Would you like me to send it?
Person: Not yet. I will send it in the fall, after we talk.
Assistant: Okay, I will keep it saved.

Ahmed was a gardener, and the morning was cold. His hands were stiff, but there was a lot to do before lunch. Now and then he forgot to rest, and his back hurt.

'Start timer,' he said to his phone. The assistant started a thirty minute work timer, which was the one he usually used.

He dug for a while and moved a heavy pot of flowers into the sun. When the timer rang, he said, 'Take a break.' The assistant understood and set a ten minute rest. It also made the phone go quiet, so no messages would bother him.

Ahmed sat on a stool with a cup of tea and watched a bird in the hedge. When the break was over, he said, 'Again,' and the timer started once more.

In an emergency, a few simple things can keep you safe. A smoke alarm makes a loud noise when it smells smoke, so you can leave the house quickly. If the power goes out, a flashlight helps in the dark. A silent house is not always a safe house, so test your alarm every month. In heavy rain, a leaf can block a drain and cause flooding in the street. If water rises, do not drive through it. People ask for help with words like call the fire brigade, turn off the alarm, or send my location to my sister. After a false alarm, they may say silence it. Know the number to call for help.

Kai was walking home from school with a package under one arm. A little earlier, his friends had taken a funny picture of a dog on a skateboard. Kai wanted to send it, but both hands were full, so he spoke to his phone.

He typed in a hurry, 'send the last pic to mom and to my frends.'

The assistant understood who he meant by mom and found the newest photo in his gallery. It showed the photo of the dog and asked, 'Is this the one?'

'Yes,' said Kai. The assistant sent it to his mom and to the group chat called Friends. Kai felt calm. He would not have to stop in the street. Soon his phone buzzed with laughing faces.

Mr. Dunn was not good with technology, but today he had to get to the dentist, and his car was in the garage. His neighbor had shown him how to use the assistant on his phone, so he tried it.

'Book me a taxi and tell me when it arrives,' he said slowly.

The assistant understood that he had asked two things. It booked a ride to the dentist's office and said it would tell him when the car was near. 'Where should the driver meet you?' it asked.

'At the front of my house,' said Mr. Dunn. 'And remind me to lock the door.'

The assistant showed the driver's name and picture on the screen. Ten minutes later it said, 'Your taxi is here.' Mr. Dunn locked the door and went out.

Privacy is about who can see what is yours. A password keeps your things closed to strangers. A good password is long and hard to guess. A word like lemon is easy for someone to try, but lemon with other words and numbers is better. A lock on your phone keeps people out if you lose it. Many people prefer a fingerprint, but on a humid day wet fingers do not always work, so they use a code. People change passwords when they think someone might know the old one. They say change my password, lock my phone, or who can see my photos? It is a good habit to keep your secret words to yourself.

Grandma Elsie liked to start her day with a walk, but her knees did not like the cold. She stood by the window, looked at the grey sky, and asked her speaker for help.

'Is it going to rain before the school bell rings this afternoon?' she asked. 'I run to pick up the children.'

The assistant understood that she meant the afternoon pick up. It said there was a small chance of rain at three, and the temperature would stay near twenty degrees.

'What should I wear?' she asked.

The assistant suggested a light coat and a small umbrella. Elsie wanted to stay healthy, so she also took a scarf. She smiled, picked up her bag, and went out into the day.

Nora came home from the hospital, tired after a night shift, and wanted a short rest before doing something she loved. She sat in her armchair with a ball of yarn and spoke to her phone.

'Could you please schedule an hour for knitting this afternoon at four? I would like to finish the next chapter of my pattern before my friend visits on Saturday, and I think I'll feel better if I plan it.'

The assistant understood that she wanted a time block. It put knitting on her calendar for four o'clock, for one hour. It also set a gentle reminder ten minutes before.

Nora thanked it. She closed her eyes for a short nap, and when the reminder came she woke up ready to knit.

Lena had just woken up, and her head was still full of sleep. The kitchen smelled like a burned piece of toast, so she knew it was not a day for cooking. She sat by the fish tank and spoke to her phone.

'Order a bagel with cream cheese and tell me how close the driver is,' she said.

The assistant opened the food delivery app. It understood that she had asked two things. First, it ordered a bagel with cream cheese from the cafe around the corner. Then it checked the map and said the driver was only four minutes away.

Lena stretched, fed the fish, and waited by the door. When the bell rang, the bagel was warm in its paper bag.

Baking turns simple things like flour, water and heat into bread, cakes and cookies. Dough needs time to rise, and then it needs the right heat. A cake might bake for forty minutes, and a batch of cookies for ten. Every oven is a little different, so people watch the clock. They change times and heat with words like ten more minutes, a bit hotter, or take it out now. You boil water for some recipes, but not for bread. A second look through the glass door can tell you if the top is golden. A straight knife in the middle of a cake should come out clean when it is ready.

- has my package come yet
- tell me when the delivery shows up
- I have band practice on the weekend, will my parcel come before then
- where did the driver leave the box
- did anything arrive from the book shop

A smart speaker is a small device that listens and plays sound. It can play music, tell you the time, and answer simple questions. It may be only one foot tall, but a heavy bass can fill a room. People often put one speaker in the kitchen and another in the bedroom. They can group speakers so the same song plays in every room. They say make it louder, lower the volume, or play in the whole house. If a speaker is not needed, they ask to disconnect it from the group. Some speakers know different voices, so they can answer each person in their own way. They are easy to move from room to room.
